questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with idiopathic (immune) thrombocytopenic purpura was listed for an elective splenectomy.
questions.lead_in: What vaccination would be most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccine Hib, meningococcal ACWY vaccine, meningococcal B vaccine, and influenza vaccines should be administered ideally ≥2 weeks before the procedure or delayed until 2 weeks afterward.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q28

questions.question: Conditions indicated in – complement deficiency (eculizumab), asplenic, laboratory workers, during menB outbreak, circumstances when could be considered (ie/ outbreak…)

parts.text: Conditions indicated in – complement deficiency (eculizumab), asplenic, laboratory workers, during menB outbreak, circumstances when could be considered (ie/ outbreak…)

questions.model_answer: MenB vaccine is indicated for: (1) Persons with complement deficiencies (including those on eculizumab/complement inhibitors). (2) Asplenic or hyposplenic individuals (anatomic or functional). (3) Laboratory personnel routinely working with N. meningitidis isolates. (4) During a declared serogroup B meningococcal outbreak (public health-directed mass vaccination). It may also be considered for close contacts of a case, travelers to areas with a MenB outbreak, and first-year college/university students living in residence, on a case-by-case/shared clinical decision-making basis.

parts.text: a) What 3 recommendations (outside of vaccines) would you make/discuss with her at the ID appointment?
b) What 4 vaccines would you give in the context of splenectomy?

cohort_answer.text:

questions.question: 60yo patient with ITP after receiving steroids and IVIG for planned splenectomy.

parts.text: Name 8 recommended vaccines according to NACI.
Name 2 vaccines that must be delayed in patient's receiving IVIG.

cohort_answer.text: 8 vaccines: PPV23, PCV13, Hib, Quadrivalent conjugated meningococcal, Meningococcal B, Influenza vaccine, Hepatitis A (for people with repeated transfusions), Hepatitis B (as above), Salmonella typhi vaccine if indicated. Vaccines to delay with IVIG: MMR and varicella

questions.question: Patient with functional asplenia comes in with septic shock following dog bite.

parts.text: What are four other conditions that cause functional asplenia.
Name two parasitic infections that this patient is at risk of.

cohort_answer.text: Other conditions causing functional asplenia: Sickle cell anaemia; Thalassemia major; Chronic liver disease; Immunodeficiencies; Malignancies; HIV; Sarcoidosis; SLE. Parasitic infections at risk: Malaria, Babesia microti

questions.question: Man with E coli meningitis with rapidly expanding perianal rash.

parts.text: What is the likely cause?
Two infectious risk factors for this.
Two non-infectious risk factors for this.
3 Diagnostic tests (name 3).
What are the precautions.

cohort_answer.text: Likely cause: Disseminated Strongyloides. Infectious risk factors: HTLV, HIV-1. Non-infectious risk factors: SOT, anti-TNF drugs, hypogammaglobulinemia, high dose steroids, haematological malignancy. Diagnostic tests: Serology; Stool for O&P (larvae); CSF, urine, blood O&P; BAL for larvae; Agar plate culture. Precautions: Contact precautions because disseminated strongy

questions.question: A 15-year-old girl with refractory ITP is going for splenectomy in 4 months.

parts.text: List 6 vaccines she needs, and the timing of administration
Other than vaccine, what are two methods to prevent infection?
What pathogens cause severe disease if an asplenic patient is bitten by a dog?
What pathogens cause severe disease if an asplenic patient is bitten by a tick in New England?

cohort_answer.text: Vaccines (ideally at least 2 weeks, ideally 10-12 weeks prior to splenectomy): PCV-13 anytime from now; PPV-23 8 weeks after PCV-13; Men B-4C now and second dose 4-8 weeks later; Men ACYW-135 now and second dose 8 weeks later; Haemophilus Type B (regardless of vaccination history); Annual influenza vaccination; all other routine immunizations (HepB, HPV). Other prevention: Daily antimicrobial prophylaxis (beta lactam) for at least 2 years post-splenectomy (adults 1 year), abortive/pill-in-pocket beta lactams, patient/family education, malaria prophylaxis if traveling. Dog bite pathogen: Capnocytophaga canimorsus. New England tick bite pathogen: Babesia microti

questions.question: 5 year old with ITP who is planning to get splenectomy.

parts.text: What are 8 vaccinates as recommended by NACI
How long before the splenectomy should the patient receive the vaccines
What 2 vaccines would you need to delay if given IVIG

questions.model_answer: a) Eight NACI-recommended vaccines prior to splenectomy: (1) Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13/PCV20). (2) Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23). (3) Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) conjugate vaccine. (4) Meningococcal ACYW conjugate vaccine. (5) Meningococcal B vaccine. (6) Annual inactivated influenza vaccine. (7) Age-appropriate routine childhood immunizations kept up to date (e.g. DTaP-IPV). (8) COVID-19 vaccine per current schedule. b) Timing: complete vaccine series at least 2 weeks before elective splenectomy (to allow adequate immune response before loss of splenic function). c) Vaccines to delay if given IVIG: live vaccines - MMR (measles-mumps-rubella) and varicella vaccine (passive antibody in IVIG can blunt immune response; delay typically 8-11 months depending on IVIG dose).
questions.beyond_mandell: NACI Canadian Immunization Guide - immunization of persons with asplenia

questions.question: 15 years old going for splenectomy in 4 months

parts.text: 5 vaccines he needs, timing of administration
Other than vaccine, 2 methods for prevention
What bug are you concerned about if asplenic patient is bitten by dog
What bug are you concerned about if asplenic patient is bitten by tick in New England

cohort_answer.text: 5 vaccines/timing: Ideally give vaccines up to 2 weeks before splenectomy; Conjugated quadrivalent meningococcal vaccine, 2 doses, 8 wks apart; Meningococcal B vaccine (Bexsero) 1st dose then 2nd dose 2 months later; PCV13, PPV23 (Pneumovax) 8 weeks later; HiB at least 2 weeks before surgery; Flu at start of season. Other prevention methods: Penicillin/amoxicillin prophylaxis x 2 years post splenectomy; Malaria ppx. Bitten by dog: Capnocytophaga canimorsus. Bitten by tick in New England: Babesia microti

questions.question: Patient with refractory ITP on steroids and IVIG

parts.text: Name 8 vaccines to give or ensure are updated prior to splenectomy.
Name two vaccines impacted by receipt of IVIg.

cohort_answer.text: Vaccines (>=2 weeks prior, ideally 10-12 weeks): Prevnar (PCV-13), Pneumovax (PPV-23, >=8 weeks later), N. meningitidis (A,C,Y,W135), N. meningitidis (B), H. influenzae Type B, Influenza (annual); also MMR, VZV (Zostavax/Shingrix), Varicella if no immunity, TDap, HepB, HPV. IVIg-impacted vaccines: MMR and Varicella (live vaccines inactivated by IVIg) - give either >=2 weeks before or >=3-11 months after IVIG depending on dosage

questions.question: Functional asplenia

parts.text: Name immunologic deficits secondary to asplenia/hyposplenia
Name 4 causes of asplenia
Name two parasites that may cause severe infection in asplenic patients

cohort_answer.text: Immunologic deficits: filtration/clearance deficit, adaptive immunity deficit, generation of IgM/IgG to polysaccharides (T cell independent), innate immunity (marginal zone macrophage scavengers). Causes: Congenital asplenia (cyanotic congenital HD), Acquired traumatic (MVC), Acquired infarction (sickle cell disease), Acquired planned surgical resection (ITP), acquired functional hyposplenia (GVHD/HIV/Celiac/SLE). Parasites: Babesia spp., Malaria (bacteria: HiB, S. pneumo, N. meningitidis, C. canimorsus, Salmonella, Bordetella)

questions.question: Woman with splenectomy.

parts.text: Name 4 things other than vaccines to discuss with her.
What 4 vaccines are indicated?

questions.model_answer: a) Four non-vaccine counseling points: (1) Risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI) - seek urgent medical attention for any fever. (2) Antibiotic prophylaxis (e.g. penicillin V or amoxicillin), particularly in the first 1-2 years post-splenectomy or lifelong in high-risk patients. (3) Carry an emergency antibiotic supply for empiric self-treatment with fever if unable to access care promptly (e.g. when travelling). (4) Malaria/babesiosis risk counseling - avoid or take precautions in endemic travel areas, and inform healthcare providers/wear medical alert identification of asplenia status. b) Four indicated vaccines: pneumococcal (PCV + PPSV23), Haemophilus influenzae type b, meningococcal ACYW conjugate, meningococcal B (plus annual influenza).

questions.question: A 60 F was recently dx with ITP 2 weeks ago. She was started on IVIG & steroids. There are plans for a splenectomy. (Alternate stem: 15 year old who had splenectomy for ITP.)

parts.text: Name the 8 vaccines recommended that a patient receive prior to splenectomy per NACI
When should these vaccines be given in relation to the splenectomy (ie how long before splenectomy)?
Which 2 vaccines would be impacted by her receiving IVIG?

cohort_answer.text: A) All routine immunizations + yearly influenza + COVID; S. pneumo (Prevnar/pneumovax, current recommendations: not previously vaccinated - PCV20 or PCV15+PPSV23 ≥8 weeks later; previously vaccinated - varies); HiB (1 dose for all patients after age 5 irrespective of prior status); Meningococcal (Men-ACYW and MenB); annual influenza; typhoid vaccine if travel to endemic regions; Hep A; Hep B (if repeat transfusions needed); other routine (DPT, Polio, MMR, VZV, rotavirus for kids, HPV for teens). B) Ideally 2 weeks before elective splenectomy; if emergent, begin vaccines 2 weeks after. C) MMR; VZV (live attenuated zostervax) - live vaccine efficacy may decrease if given ~2 weeks before or 8-11 months after IVIG.

parts.text: Name four causes of functional asplenia
Name two parasitic diseases that are more severe in these patients

questions.model_answer: a) Four causes of functional asplenia: (1) Sickle cell disease (autoinfarction). (2) Celiac disease. (3) Inflammatory bowel disease (e.g. ulcerative colitis). (4) Splenic irradiation or infiltrative disease (e.g. amyloidosis, sarcoidosis) causing splenic hypofunction; graft-versus-host disease also accepted. b) Two parasitic diseases more severe in asplenic/hyposplenic patients: babesiosis and malaria (both intraerythrocytic parasites, spleen critical for clearance).

questions.question: 14 year old from Philippines immigrated 1 year ago. Splenectomy 2 weeks ago after car accident.

parts.text: Other than immunizations, what 4 things should you discuss at this meeting?

cohort_answer.text: 1. Antibiotic ppx - ideally lifelong amoxicillin 250mg PO BID. 2. Emergency antibiotic supply - present to hospital at first fever/infection sign, consider pill-in-pocket amoxclav. 3. Travel precautions - malaria ppx if travelling to endemic regions, avoid mosquito/tick bites. 4. Animal bites - abx ppx needed for dog bite (C. canimorsus). 5. Other - med alert card or bracelet.

questions.question: Splenectomized 26 year old man. Should you give the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, the polysaccharide vaccine, or both? Explain.

parts.text: Should you give conjugate, polysaccharide, or both? Explain

questions.model_answer: Give both. Rationale: pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13/PCV20) induces T-cell dependent immune memory and a more robust, longer-lasting response, and should be given first; pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) broadens serotype coverage (23 serotypes vs 13-20 in conjugate) but produces a T-cell independent, less durable response without immune memory. In asplenic patients (high risk for encapsulated organism sepsis), sequential administration - PCV first, followed by PPSV23 at least 8 weeks later - maximizes both magnitude/durability of response and serotype breadth.

questions.question: You have a patient who is going for splenectomy for TTP. Make a vaccine schedule with the list of vaccines (menC conjugate, tetravalent polysaccharide, 7-valent conjugate, 23 valent polysaccharide, influenza, typhoid vaccine, HiB, MMR). You can use each vaccine never, once, or more than once. Make the schedule for before the operation and for 1 year after.

parts.text: Make a vaccine schedule before the operation and for 1 year after

cohort_answer.text: 2 weeks pre-op (or 2 weeks post-op if emergent): Pneu-C-20 (single dose) OR PCV13/15; HiB (regardless of prior vaccination); Men-C-ACYW; Men-B. 8-10 weeks post initial vaccines: Pneu-P-23 (only if PCV13/15); Men-C-ACYW 2nd dose; Men-B 2nd dose. 1 year after: ACYW q5years and MenB 1 year after completion of primary series and q2-3years thereafter; annual influenza + COVID; typhoid vaccine if travel to endemic areas.

questions.question: Name the most likely pathogen for the following scenarios.

parts.text: AML patient with central venous catheter with sepsis and haemorrhagic bullous skin lesions. The aspirate is growing a GPR.
Asplenic patient with sepsis after dog bite.
Necrotizing scalp infection after swimming.
CVID patient with chronic abdominal pain and diarrhea.

questions.model_answer: a) AML patient with CVC, sepsis, hemorrhagic bullous lesions, GPR growing on aspirate: most likely Bacillus cereus (or consider Clostridium species) - hemorrhagic bullae in neutropenic host with CVC and gram-positive rod strongly suggests Bacillus cereus bacteremia. b) Asplenic patient with sepsis after dog bite: Capnocytophaga canimorsus. c) Necrotizing scalp infection after swimming: Aeromonas hydrophila (freshwater exposure) - consider Vibrio vulnificus if saltwater exposure. d) CVID patient with chronic abdominal pain/diarrhea: Giardia lamblia.

questions.question: PM 14. What is the most likely organism to the species level in the following situations? AML with CVC and hemorrhagic bullae with GPB? (1); Fresh water exposure and necrotizing scalp cellulitis (1); CVID on interferon gamma with bloating and diarrhea (1); Post splenectomy patient who gets sepsis following a dog bite (1)

parts.text: AML with CVC and hemorrhagic bullae with GPB?
Fresh water exposure and necrotizing scalp cellulitis
CVID on interferon gamma with bloating and diarrhea
Post splenectomy patient who gets sepsis following a dog bite

cohort_answer.text: Clostridium septicum (in immunocompromised can cause gas gangrene without trauma, differentiating from C. perfringens; translocates from GI to hematogenous spread to skin; associated with colorectal CA). Aeromonas hydrophila (fresh water). Giardia lamblia/duodenalis. Capnocytophaga canimorsus.
